scenes.headline: pandas: Series & DataFrames
scenes.subtitle: The core data structures for tabular data
scenes.narration: pandas is the workhorse of Python data work, and everything it does rests on two foundational structures: the one-dimensional Series and the two-dimensional DataFrame.

scenes.headline: Series vs DataFrame
scenes.narration: A Series is a single labeled column of data, essentially a one-dimensional array paired with an index. A DataFrame is a two-dimensional table with many columns, each of which is itself a Series, all sharing the same row index. Thinking of a DataFrame as a dictionary of aligned Series is the mental model that makes the rest of pandas click.

scenes.headline: Creating a DataFrame
scenes.narration: You can construct a DataFrame directly from a dictionary where each key becomes a column and each list becomes its values. In practice you far more often load one straight from a source using a reader like read_csv, and pandas offers matching readers for JSON, Parquet, SQL, and many other formats. Either way, the result is the same tabular structure ready to work with.

scenes.headline: Inspecting data
scenes.narration: The head and tail methods let you eyeball the first or last rows without printing the whole frame. The info and describe methods reveal column types, null counts, and summary statistics in one glance. Checking shape and dtypes confirms the size and the type of every column, while columns and index expose the labels. Starting every analysis with this inspection catches surprises before they become bugs.

scenes.headline: Selecting with loc & iloc
scenes.code:
df['spend']            # a Series
df[['user', 'spend']]  # a DataFrame
df.loc[df.spend > 10]  # boolean filter by label
df.iloc[0:2]           # by integer position
scenes.narration: Selecting a single column with bracket access returns a Series, while passing a list of names returns a smaller DataFrame. The loc accessor selects by label and pairs naturally with boolean masks, so here it keeps only rows where spend exceeds ten. The iloc accessor selects by integer position instead, which is useful when you care about location rather than labels.

scenes.headline: Typical workflow
scenes.narration: Nearly every pandas task follows the same rhythm. You load the data, inspect it to understand its shape and quality, select or filter down to the rows and columns you care about, and then transform what remains into the result you need.

scenes.text: A DataFrame is aligned Series; use loc for labels, iloc for positions, and boolean masks to filter.
scenes.narration: Once you internalize that a DataFrame is just aligned Series and master selection with loc, iloc, and boolean masks, the rest of pandas falls into place.
